newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Audi seeks U.S. revival after sales plunge.
newsitem.headline: Audi seeks U.S. revival after sales plunge.

text.p: German automaker Audi AG is back on the road in the lucrative U.S. market after recovering from a sharp slowdown in sales 10 years ago following allegations that its luxury sedan could have unintended acceleration problems.

U.S. officials cleared Audi of the allegations, made in a 1986 television programme, a few years later but the damage was done. Its U.S. sales skidded to 12,283 vehicles in 1991 from a 1985 peak of more than 74,000.

But Audi's U.S. sales last year were the best in a decade, rising to 27,379 cars, which represented a doubling of sales in two years. The gains made Audi, part of the Volkswagen group, the fastest-growing luxury car maker in America.
Its current sales still lag those of the heady days of the 1980s but more good times appear to be ahead.
The company predicts 20 percent growth in 1997 sales to slightly more than 30,000 vehicles.
"We still have a way to go and we will keep up the aggressive growth," Gerd Klauss, the architect of Audi's recovery in North America, said in a recent telephone interview from its Detroit office.

Renewed growth has come from strong consumer interest in Audi's A4 and A8 sedans. Audi officials hope to add fuel to the expansion with the new A6 sedan, which will be unveiled this week at the Geneva car show.

The A6 targets affluent buyers who are also considering such cars as the BMW 5-series and the Mercedes E-Class sedans. It will be available for German delivery in May and Audi will announce in Geneva when it will be sent to the U.S. market.
